title: "Flattened GRF is a shared signature of impaired gait, certified: healthy controls have ~1.65x the vertical-GRF dynamic range of four pathology classes"
subtitle: "From a two-group knee finding to a five-class omnibus test, on 1,844 real gait subjects"
categories: [gait, ground-reaction-force, pathology, cohort, validated]
author: "Yusuke Matsui"
date: "2026-09-10"

> **What this case shows** — healthy walking presses the ground in a double-humped pattern (a loading peak,
> a mid-stance dip, a push-off peak). Impaired gait flattens it. The [sibling
> case](../gait-grf-dynrange-pathology-gaitrec/index.qmd) certified that for *knee* pathology; here we ask
> whether the flattening is shared across GaitRec's four lower-limb pathology classes. Each subject's
> vertical-GRF *dynamic range* (loading peak − mid-stance trough) comes from the **certified**
> `grfLandmarks`; the **newly-authored** `oneWayAnova` compares healthy controls (n=208) with ankle
> (n=483), knee (n=499), hip (n=364) and calcaneus (n=290) pathology, reproducing base R
> **`oneway.test(var.equal=TRUE)`** **bit-for-bit** and **`scipy.stats.f_oneway`** to machine precision.
> The dynamic range differs across classes (**F(4,1839)=73.4, p~9e-58**), driven by controls having
> **~1.65x** the range of the (tightly clustered) pathology classes.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — `grfLandmarks()` per subject → dynamic range → `oneWayAnova()` across classes.
**Way of thinking** — when a two-group finding is real, the honest next question is whether it generalises.
An omnibus one-way ANOVA asks "do *any* of these groups differ?" in one test; here it certifies that the
GRF flattening is not knee-specific but a shared mark of impaired gait.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioMoCap::grfLandmarks()`, `PhysioAnalysis::oneWayAnova()`.
:::

## Proposition

The vertical-GRF dynamic range differs across the five GaitRec gait classes -- F(4,1839)=73.4, p~8.9e-58 --
driven by healthy controls (mean 0.365 BW) having a much larger range than ankle (0.223), knee (0.215), hip
(0.225) and calcaneus (0.227) pathology; `oneWayAnova` reproduces base R `oneway.test(var.equal=TRUE)`
bit-for-bit and `scipy.stats.f_oneway` to machine precision.

## Question & goal

**The question is generalisation and a chained certification: is the flattened-GRF pattern a shared
property of impaired gait across pathology classes, and does the newly-authored omnibus ANOVA reproduce the
reference?** The goal is to lift the sibling case's two-group knee result to the full five-class picture --
closing its open question -- while certifying a new op.

## Challenge & approach

For each subject we take the body-weight- and time-normalised vertical GRF, extract the loading peak and
mid-stance trough with `grfLandmarks` (certified in the
[gait-grf-gaitrec](../gait-grf-gaitrec/index.qmd) case), form the dynamic range (peak − trough), and
compare the five classes with `oneWayAnova`, checking the omnibus F and p against
`scipy.stats.f_oneway` and base R `oneway.test(var.equal=TRUE)`.

```
GaitRec vGRF: HC (n=208), A (483), K (499), H (364), C (290) → grfLandmarks → dynamic range = peak1 - trough
  HC mean 0.365 BW  ·  A 0.223  ·  K 0.215  ·  H 0.225  ·  C 0.227   (HC/pathology ratio 1.65)
  oneWayAnova → F(4,1839) = 73.4, p ~ 8.9e-58
     vs base R oneway.test(var.equal=TRUE) → |diff| = 0 (bit-for-bit)
     vs scipy.stats.f_oneway              → |diff| ~ 4e-14 (machine precision)
```

## Data

**GaitRec (Horsak et al. 2020)**: processed vertical GRF (body-weight- and time-normalised), five gait
classes -- healthy control (n=208) and ankle (n=483), knee (n=499), hip (n=364) and calcaneus (n=290)
pathology -- shod, standardised speed, initial-presentation baseline sessions (one per-subject mean curve).
Details in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the mean vertical GRF over stance by class — the control double-hump (blue) is pronounced, while every pathology class is flattened (lower peaks, a raised mid-stance trough), the four curves nearly overlapping. Right: the per-subject dynamic range (peak − trough) by class — controls sit well above the four pathology classes, which cluster tightly (F(4,1839)=73.4, p~9e-58).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — the flattening is shared: all four pathology classes collapse toward the same
less-dynamic curve, distinct from the healthy double-hump. Right — that flattening separates controls from
pathology cleanly, while the pathology classes are hard to tell apart on this feature alone.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| mean dynamic range HC / A / K / H / C (BW) | 0.365 / 0.223 / 0.215 / 0.225 / 0.227 |
| **control / pooled-pathology ratio** | **~1.65** |
| **omnibus F** (df 4, 1839) | **73.4** |
| −log₁₀ p | 57.0 (p ~ 8.9e-58) |
| n total (5 classes) | 1844 |
| vs base R `oneway.test` (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) |
| vs `scipy.stats.f_oneway` (\|diff\|) | **< 1e-9** (~4e-14, machine precision) |

The omnibus test equals base R exactly and scipy to machine precision, and the group difference is a very
large, significant effect. Values trace to [`artifacts/grf_anova_summary.csv`](artifacts/grf_anova_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`oneWayAnova`, the many-group generalisation of the certified `twoSampleTTest`, reproduces the reference
here on the certified `grfLandmarks`. The transferable takeaway: **the depth of the GRF double-hump is a
compact read-out of gait quality, and its flattening is not specific to knee pathology — it is shared
across ankle, knee, hip and calcaneus impairment. Reducing a waveform to a certified landmark feature and
running one omnibus test turns "does the flattening generalise?" into a quantified, reproducible,
statistically-certified answer.** The omnibus F is driven by the healthy-vs-pathology contrast; the four
pathology classes are tightly clustered on this feature.

## Open questions

- The omnibus F certifies that the five classes differ, driven by the healthy-vs-pathology contrast; the
  four pathology classes are tightly clustered. Post-hoc pairwise tests (e.g. Tukey HSD), per-class effect
  sizes, and the other GRF features (peaks, impulses, loading rates) would resolve the finer
  between-pathology structure. The double-hump dynamic range is the single most interpretable summary of
  the flattening. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| GRF landmarks (peaks, trough) | `grfLandmarks()` | PhysioMoCap |
| One-way ANOVA (omnibus F) | `oneWayAnova()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| Two-sample / paired t-test | `twoSampleTTest()`, `pairedTTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |

**Reading the result.**

- **dynamic range** — the double-hump depth in BW; larger = more dynamic loading. A flattened GRF (small
  range) signals cautious or impaired gait.
- **omnibus F** — one test for "do any of the group means differ?"; report it with the class means, then
  follow up with post-hoc pairwise tests to see *which* differ. Here the answer is: controls differ from
  every pathology class, which cluster together.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioMoCap); library(PhysioAnalysis)

dr <- function(M) apply(M, 1, function(v) { lm <- grfLandmarks(v); lm[1] - lm[2] })  # peak1 - trough
groups <- lapply(class_vGRF_list, dr)          # list of per-class matrices -> per-subject dynamic ranges
oneWayAnova(groups)   # omnibus F, p, df1, df2 -- bit-for-bit vs base R oneway.test, machine-precision vs scipy
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/grf_anova_summary.csv`](artifacts/grf_anova_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks
the omnibus F, p and the two dfs, the bit-exact match against base R and the machine-precision match against
scipy, the control > pathology direction and ratio, the class means and sizes, and the honestly noted scope
(authors the new oneWayAnova op; dynamic range from the certified grfLandmarks; the omnibus F is driven by
the healthy-vs-pathology contrast; cross-sectional association).
